title: Closed-loop control for two-qubit gates with trapped ions
authors: Eduardo J. Páez, Seyed Shakib Vedaie, Barry C. Sanders
abstract: State-of-the-art two-qubit gates with trapped ions employ open-loop control that rely on simplified models to precompute control sequences. Our aim is to introduce closed-loop control for two-qubit gates to correct disturbances as they occur during the gate implementation. We introduce a spectator ion into the ion chain used for quantum logic processing, where it couples with the other ions through collective motional modes. The spectator ion's position is continuously monitored by driving dipole transitions and detecting the resultant fluorescence. We show that incorporating a spectator ion is feasible for linear Paul trap implementations and is expected to reduce the two-qubit gate Bell-state preparation infidelity by an order of magnitude with the deleterious effects of position monitoring being negligible compared to the thermal effects that exist in the system, even in the absence of the spectator ions. Mathematically, we describe driven ion-trap dynamics, including the spectator ion, by a stochastic quantum master equation involving the amplitude-modulation multimode-motional coupling gate, motional drift, thermal effects, recoil from photon scattering, spontaneous decay, and light shift. Our on-the-fly control method employs reinforcement learning with the reward function based on the actual geometric phase of the spectator ion. A key advantage of our approach is that we introduce a control method that involves `learning' and correcting disturbances happening in the trap on-the-fly, thus achieving high-fidelity gates. Our approach will lead to a significantly higher two-qubit gate fidelity at a reduced calibration overhead owing to the small parameter drift in the control system.
summary: This paper proposes a novel closed-loop control scheme for two-qubit gates in trapped ion quantum processors. By introducing and continuously monitoring an ancillary 'spectator' ion, the system can actively correct for environmental disturbances like motional drift in real time. This approach, implemented using reinforcement learning, promises substantially higher gate fidelity with reduced calibration overhead compared to existing open-loop techniques.
main_problem: The primary goal is to enhance the fidelity of two-qubit gates (2QG) in trapped ions by implementing a closed-loop control mechanism that actively corrects for real-time system disturbances.
main_result: A closed-loop, reinforcement learning approach utilizing continuous monitoring of a spectator ion can significantly reduce 2QG gate infidelity by an order of magnitude compared to current open-loop methods.
method: The authors employ quantum trajectory theory (QTT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL), specifically using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), to train a control policy that adjusts laser pulses on the fly based on measured ion position.
model_or_system: The system is trapped ions in a linear Paul trap, where gate operations are mediated by collective motional modes. The dynamics are modeled via a stochastic quantum master equation incorporating various noise sources like thermal effects and motional drift.
key_observables: Two-qubit gate Bell-state preparation infidelity, spectator ion position (monitored via fluorescence), and the geometric phase accumulated during the gate.
important_parameters:
The fidelity improvement is quantified relative to current state-of-the-art methods; key parameters include Rabi frequencies ($\Omega$), detunings ($\mu$), and motional frequencies ($
u$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that continuous position monitoring is feasible and its impact on infidelity is negligible compared to inherent thermal effects. The control scheme relies on mapping measured positions to optimal laser intensities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate pulse sequences, corresponding phase-space trajectories for multiple motional modes (CoM, tilt mode), and the overall architecture of the closed-loop monitoring system involving electronics like FPGAs.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the limitations of open-loop control to introducing the spectator ion mechanism. It details the mathematical modeling using stochastic master equations, presents the RL framework for policy generation, and concludes by demonstrating the feasibility and performance gains of the closed-loop scheme.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant step toward fault-tolerant quantum computation in trapped ions by moving beyond idealized Hamiltonian descriptions to incorporate real-world noise sources via active feedback control. The combination of advanced quantum optics modeling with machine learning for control is highly relevant.

Figure 2. Diagram of the CLPM-scheme. A three-ion chain is illustrated, where the orange dots represent gate ions and the green dot represents the spectator ion. The spectator ion is illuminated with an external coherent laser coupled to the 2S1/2 – 2P1/2 transition, illustrated as a diagonal blue cone-like shape. An array of lenses and a back mirror collect and su- perpose the fluorescence light to undergo a two-channel time- correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) setup. The out- put signal is sent to a FPGA for post-processing. The global and bichromatic Raman beams are not shown for simplicity.
